Patient demographics:

  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Animals: Dogs, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Vignette:
Priya, a sixty-one-year-old woman with hands weathered from decades of farm work, described the past eight months as living in a different world, one superimposed over the familiar landscape of her life. The event that fractured her reality occurred on a late afternoon in spring, as she was walking the perimeter of the fields where she worked. A man had emerged from the sparse line of trees bordering the property, two lean, barking dogs at his side. The assault itself was a blur of pain and terror, but the sensory details remained impossibly sharp: the smell of dry dust, the weight of his body, and most of all, the incessant, frantic barking of the dogs circling just feet away. This memory was not something she recalled; it was something that happened to her, again and again.

In the weeks that followed, Priya’s world began to shrink. The first thing to go was sleep. She would lie awake for hours, her body rigid, convinced that every rustle of leaves outside was a footstep. She had come to believe that only by remaining vigilant could she prevent another attack, so she would watch the dawn creep into the sky before exhaustion finally claimed her for an hour or two. Her husband, Raj, would try to comfort her, but his touch became a source of alarm. If he reached for her in the night, even gently, she would jolt away with a gasp, her heart hammering against her ribs. She explained that her body simply reacted before her mind had a chance to catch up, a reflex she couldn't control. After she inadvertently struck him one night, they began sleeping in separate rooms. Intimacy of any kind became unthinkable, a door she had sealed and barricaded.

Her work, once a source of quiet pride, became a minefield. The open fields, the angle of the afternoon sun, the scent of turned earth—any of these things could, without warning, plunge her back into the memory. When this happened, it was not like watching a film; she was there again, on the ground, the terror as fresh and absolute as it was that day. The memory would play on a loop in her mind, a relentless replay of the worst moments of her life. Her greatest fear, however, was dogs. The sight of any dog, even a small one on a leash across the street, would trigger a primal, physical response. Her breath would catch, her muscles would seize, and she would be frozen in place, her body bracing for an attack that her rational mind knew wasn't coming. She started taking a longer route to the farm to avoid a house with a yapping terrier, adding thirty minutes to her walk each way. This avoidance cost her time and energy, but it felt like a necessary sacrifice for a sliver of safety.

The decision to seek help came after a visit from her daughter and five-year-old granddaughter. Priya was in the kitchen when the little girl ran up and hugged her legs from behind. The unexpected touch sent a shockwave of panic through her. She cried out and stumbled away, knocking over a chair. The look of fear and confusion on her granddaughter’s face was more painful than anything she had experienced since the assault. It was in that moment she realised the fortress she had built to protect herself was now imprisoning her and hurting the people she loved most. She came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a desperate plea to stop being a source of fear for her own family. She was terrified that the woman she used to be was gone forever, but a small part of her held on to the possibility that she might one day be able to hold her husband's hand or accept a hug from her grandchild without her body screaming danger.
